segments.text: Part zero three: From nineteen forty to nineteen fifty-nine. Chapter eight: Rebel Youth.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The 1950s ushered in a new era of bikers, film noir and rebellious youth.
segments.text: The nineteen fifties ushered in a new era of bikers, film noir and rebellious youth.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Between the release of The Wild One (1953) and Easy Rider (1969), Hollywood entered into a long and troubled relationship with American youth, explaining, indulging and exploiting the phenomenon of adolescence. Although important in their day, these teen-oriented films are by definition ephemeral, and only a few managed to make the theme of the mid-twentieth-century generation gap endure.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The Wild One, directed by László Benedek (1905-1992), is generally considered the starting point of this phase, although it is only tangentially aimed at a teenage audience; the film's bikers seem more like outlaw cowboys than rebellious teenagers. Marlon Brando (1924-2004) was almost 30 when he made the film, but his inarticulate grace, along with his sunglasses, his leather jacket and his air of vague superiority, made him, for a brief time, the symbol of disaffected youth.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Several productions followed The Wild One in the 1990s, among them Motorcycle Gang (1957) and the underground film Scorpio Rising (1964), directed by Kenneth Anger (b. 1927). But biker movies only emerged as a subgenre after the success of Roger Corman's The Wild Angels (1966). Variations featured female gangs in The Mini-Skirt Mob (1968) and bikers in The Losers (1970); there was also the self-explanatory Werewolves on Wheels (1971). The Wild Angels also inspired Easy Rider (1969), a more artistic film that gave rise to the road movies of the 1970s, including Electra Glide in Blue (1973). Biker films remain nostalgic; the formula also gave rise to the TV series Sons of Anarchy (2008-2014).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: James Dean (1931-1955) replaced Brando's intermittent intensity with an introspective hurt. In his first major film, East of Eden (1955), directed by Elia Kazan (1909-2003), Dean's portrayal of an unstable son fighting for his father's love hit young audiences of the mid-1950s hard. Released the same year, the urban drama Rebel Without a Cause (1955), directed by Nicholas Ray (1911-1979), took the world of juvenile delinquency off the streets and brought it into a prosperous middle-class neighborhood. The film also gave Dean the role with which he is most identified. His Jim Stark is not so much a rebel; he simply does not understand the world around him.

segments.original: In Blackboard Jungle (1955), Richard Brooks (1912-1992) brings juvenile delinquency back into the inner-city school system. With a touch of well-meaning social criticism, and Glenn Ford as a teacher forced to confront his delinquent students, the film was overshadowed by its inclusion of Bill Haley's song "Rock Around the Clock".

segments.original: It was the first major Hollywood film to use rock music on its soundtrack, and in British cinemas teenagers caused disturbances at screenings of the film. In the 1950s, rock, not cinema, was the ultimate expression of youth experience, with the young Elvis Presley (1935-1977) as its charismatic god.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Presley's film career began with dramatic roles; Jailhouse Rock (1957) was one of the few films to capture the rawness of his early years. After his Army service, his acting career went into decline, with a string of good-guy roles in increasingly tedious musicals.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Too amorphous to be considered a genre, these 1950s films seem to show that Hollywood was trying to understand and exploit both the new generation and the discontents of youth. James Dean's brief career produced one of the definitive portrayals of America's mid-twentieth-century rebel generation. His death, before the release of Rebel Without a Cause, forever fixed his image as an anguished, lost teenager.

segments.original: By the mid-1960s, the emerging counterculture had changed productions aimed at teenagers. In 1966, Roger Corman (b. 1926) directed biker films such as The Wild Angels (1966). Featuring a gang of rapists and a biker's funeral with a coffin draped in a Nazi flag, The Wild Angels is far more confrontational than The Wild One.
